sources.title: history argument lecture.pdf
sources.section: Page 1 — Write an evidence-supported history argument
sources.text: This fictional teaching source describes a nineteenth-century town. A mill inspector recorded twelve-hour shifts in 1840. A workers' petition in 1842 requested ten-hour shifts, citing exhaustion. The mill owner's 1842 ledger records rising production but no shift-length change. These sources support the claim that workers sought shorter hours despite rising output; they do not establish that the demand succeeded or that every town had the same conditions.

questions.prompt: Based on the source, what claim about workers' conditions can you support?
questions.answer: Workers sought shorter hours because they were exhausted, even though production was rising.
requiredIdeas: workers wanted ten-hour shifts or shorter hours
production was rising in the owner's ledger
questions.explanation: A supported claim must stay within what the sources show: workers asked for shorter hours and said they were exhausted, while the ledger shows production was rising. That supports the idea of workers' demands despite rising output, but not that the demand succeeded.
hints: Look for what the petition requested.
Use the ledger only for what it directly shows.
Do not claim the change happened unless the source says so.
questions.workedExample: If a petition asks for safer conditions and a factory record shows accidents were still happening, you can argue workers wanted safer conditions despite ongoing production.
workedSolution: State the workers' request.
Add the reason given in the petition.
Use the ledger to show production was rising.
Avoid claiming the shorter hours were granted.

questions.prompt: Which statement is supported by the source?
questions.answer: Workers asked for ten-hour shifts because they were exhausted, even as production increased.
questions.explanation: The source supports a limited conclusion: workers requested shorter hours and explained why, while the owner's ledger shows production rose. It does not prove the request was accepted, so avoid that stronger claim.
hints: Find the petition's request.
Find the owner's record about production.
Choose the statement that matches both without adding extra claims.
workedSolution: Identify the petition's demand for ten-hour shifts.
Note the stated reason: exhaustion.
Include the ledger's rising production.
Do not add that the town was typical or that the demand succeeded.

session.methodReason: You prefer examples and hints in a short focus window, so this check has two questions.

knowledgeTopics.title: Function inputs and outputs
knowledgeTopics.description: Interpret the input and output of a function written as f(x).

explanations.text: In function notation, f(x) means the function f takes x as the input and gives an output. The value inside the parentheses is the input. The expression f(x) is the output that results after applying the function rule to that input. For example, if f(x)=x+3, then x=2 is the input and f(2)=5 is the output. A common mistake is to think f(x) means multiplication; it does not.

questions.prompt: What does the x in f(x) represent?
choices: The function’s output
The function’s input
The name of the function
requiredIdeas: x is the input to the function
f(x) is the output, not x
questions.explanation: The symbol inside the parentheses is the input value. f(x) is the result after the function acts on that input.
hints: Look at what is inside the parentheses.
Ask what value is being put into the function.
questions.workedExample: If f(4)=9, then 4 is the input and 9 is the output.
workedSolution: The x in f(x) is the input.
The function uses x to produce the output.

questions.prompt: If f(3)=10, what is the output when the input is 3?
requiredIdeas: f(3) gives the output for input 3
The output is the value after applying the function
questions.explanation: The notation f(3) already tells you the input is 3. The value on the right side, 10, is the output.
hints: Read f(3) as “the function at 3.”
The number after the equals sign is the output.
workedSolution: The input is 3.
Since f(3)=10, the output is 10.

sources.text: ATP hydrolysis releases free energy when ATP reacts with water to form ADP and inorganic phosphate. Cells couple this favorable reaction to processes that require energy. ATP is regenerated from ADP and phosphate using energy from other reactions.

knowledgeTopics.description: Explain how ATP hydrolysis supplies energy for coupled cellular work.

questions.prompt: Which statement best explains how cells use ATP hydrolysis?
choices: ATP hydrolysis releases free energy that can be coupled to energy-requiring cellular processes.
ATP hydrolysis stores energy by turning ADP into ATP.
ATP hydrolysis happens only when cells do not need energy.
ATP hydrolysis directly creates glucose for the cell.
questions.answer: ATP hydrolysis releases free energy that can be coupled to energy-requiring cellular processes.
requiredIdeas: That energy is used by coupling to processes that require energy
questions.explanation: The key idea is energy transfer, not energy storage. ATP hydrolysis breaks ATP down to ADP and inorganic phosphate and releases free energy, which cells couple to work that needs energy.
hints: Think about whether ATP is being broken down or built up.
Ask what happens to the released energy in the cell.
questions.workedExample: A cell needs energy to move a molecule across a membrane. It can use energy released when ATP is hydrolyzed to drive that process.
workedSolution: ATP is hydrolyzed to ADP and inorganic phosphate.
This hydrolysis releases free energy.
Cells couple that released energy to an energy-requiring process.

questions.prompt: What happens to ADP and inorganic phosphate when the cell has energy available again?
questions.answer: They are used to regenerate ATP.
requiredIdeas: ATP is regenerated from ADP and phosphate
Energy from other reactions is used to do this
questions.explanation: ATP does not only get used up; cells rebuild it. When energy from other reactions is available, ADP and inorganic phosphate are joined to make ATP again.
hints: Think about the reverse direction of the reaction.
What must be added to ADP to make ATP again?
workedSolution: ATP can be regenerated from ADP and inorganic phosphate.
This requires energy from other reactions.
So the cell rebuilds ATP when energy is available.

choices: ATP hydrolysis releases free energy that can be coupled to energy-requiring processes.
ATP hydrolysis stores energy by turning ADP into ATP.
ATP hydrolysis occurs only when no other reactions are happening.
ATP hydrolysis makes water from ATP and phosphate.
questions.answer: ATP hydrolysis releases free energy that can be coupled to energy-requiring processes.
requiredIdeas: Cells couple that released energy to processes that need energy
questions.explanation: The key idea is not that ATP itself is the energy store after hydrolysis; hydrolysis is the reaction that releases usable free energy. Cells then link that release to work that needs energy.
hints: Look for the option about released energy, not stored energy.
Think about what happens to ATP when water is added.
The correct choice should mention coupling to energy-requiring processes.
questions.workedExample: A cell uses the energy from a reaction that breaks a phosphate bond to power a transport protein.
workedSolution: ATP reacts with water to form ADP and inorganic phosphate.
That hydrolysis releases free energy.
The cell couples that release to a process that requires energy.

questions.prompt: If a cell needs to do work, what must happen to ATP after it is used?
questions.answer: ATP is regenerated from ADP and inorganic phosphate using energy from other reactions.
requiredIdeas: ATP is regenerated from ADP and inorganic phosphate
Energy from other reactions is used to rebuild ATP
questions.explanation: After ATP is spent, the cell does not keep using the same ATP molecule. It rebuilds ATP from ADP and phosphate by using energy captured from other reactions.
hints: Think about what the cell does with ADP and phosphate.
The answer should describe rebuilding ATP, not hydrolysis.
Include where the energy comes from.
workedSolution: ATP is used in a reaction and becomes ADP plus inorganic phosphate.
To keep working, the cell must make ATP again.
Energy from other reactions is used to regenerate ATP from ADP and phosphate.
